newsitem.title: UK: Toyota says UK still in running for plant.
newsitem.headline: Toyota says UK still in running for plant.

text.p: Japan's Toyota Motor Corporation said on Thursday Britain was still in the running to be the site of the automobile giant's next European plant, despite the strength of the sterling against other currencies.

Iwao Okijima, the executive vice-president of Toyota, said sterling, which is trading at a near eight-year high against the deutschemark, would not be a mitigating factor when it made its final choice of location for its new European plant.
Toyota is planning to set up a plant in Europe to make at least 200,000 units of either a small car or one of its 'B' category (smaller to medium sized) vehicles.
"Normally with sterling or any other currency we will not make an important decision like a plant opening on very short term currency fluctuations," Okijima told journalists at a news conference.
He said Toyota was in the middle of a study evaluating the cost of new plant in Europe and had received invitations from 10 countries to set up the new plant.
Okijima said a number of issues would be considered before a final decision was taken on the plant by mid-1998.

"Of course one has to consider a number of factors while deciding on the location -- infrastructure, water and electricity supply, transport, good quality labour, relationship of suppliers or whether we are welcome in the local community," he said.
He admitted that the UK was still a strong candidate. Other rumoured choices were France, Poland and Germany.
Commenting on Toyota's recent statement that it had faced unsatisfactory sales in Europe, vice-chairman Alan Marsh said the automaker planned a number of measures to tackle the problem.
"We will adopt a clear focus on certain product sectors in the European market. We are trying very hard to get our act together and treat Europe as a collective market place," he said.
Toyota is aiming to hike its European sales from a current 420,000 per annum to 600,000 by 2000.
